To achieve this transfer, the agent must preserve not only hue but also how each color functions in the image: the same hue may form a large-area material color or merely a local highlight or emissive accent, and these roles differ in their carrier surfaces, spatial extent, and distribution. The visual style agent therefore first determines the visual role of a color, and then organizes that role together with its carrier, scale, and color anchor as a = ( ρ , h , κ , s , g , ℓ ) ∈ A ℛ , a=(\rho,\,h,\,\kappa,\,s,\,g,\,\ell)\in A_{\mathcal{R}}, (5) where a a denotes one color/light allocation, ρ \rho specifies the visual role and scale of the color (e.g., dominant field color, large-area material color, medium light, small accent), h h provides the hexadecimal color anchor, κ \kappa identifies the carrier surface to which the color is attached, s s specifies the spatial extent of the color, g g specifies the color’s spatial distribution, and ℓ \ell specifies the color-attribute type (e.g., material color, material light, secondary illumination, shadow structure, accent). Based on the color/light allocation records in A ℛ A_{\mathcal{R}} , the agent abstracts concrete carriers into transferable surface types and generates corresponding extent constraints for each color. For example, a warm orange on a small luminous ornament in a reference image is described as a color accent within fine-scale luminous regions, while retaining its color anchor and restricting its coverage. When the subject or scene changes, the carrier may change, but the accent’s role, scale, and distribution remain constrained by the same record. The organization of color can therefore be reused without importing the original ornament. 3.4 Execution Pipeline: Building the Style State and Generating Images The preceding sections introduced the state design and the color-allocation rules. This section instantiates them as an auditable pipeline executed by the visual style agent. The agent first parses and integrates the reference image set ℛ \mathcal{R} into a style state S ℛ S_{\mathcal{R}} , then converts S ℛ S_{\mathcal{R}} into a style prompt p ℛ p_{\mathcal{R}} , and finally combines p ℛ p_{\mathcal{R}} with a new generation prompt to produce an image. • Structured extraction (reference image set ℛ \mathcal{R} → \rightarrow structured style evidence). To make visual observations computable and checkable, the visual style agent invokes the multimodal model Φ \Phi with the reference-image parsing protocol q q to analyze ℛ \mathcal{R} . Protocol q q instructs the model to extract rendering practices shared across the images, together with colors and their carriers. The protocol also instructs the model to record subjects, props, and scenes that must not be transferred. Based on the extracted information, the model outputs style evidence in a structured format (e.g., JSON), organized into four categories: rendering M ℛ M_{\mathcal{R}} , color and light A ℛ A_{\mathcal{R}} , composition T ℛ T_{\mathcal{R}} , and reference content L ℛ L_{\mathcal{R}} . To ensure structural validity and prevent reference-content leakage, the agent validates the evidence before passing it to subsequent modules. All required fields must be present, and each color record must include both a color and its carrier surface. Rendering descriptions must exclude reference subjects, props, and scenes. • Color and luminance statistics (reference image set ℛ \mathcal{R} → \rightarrow color and luminance distribution). To supplement global tonal information that is difficult to assess reliably from language alone, the visual style agent invokes the color and luminance statistics module H H . It computes luminance, saturation, hue, and dominant color clusters over ℛ \mathcal{R} , and summarizes them as global value, chroma, dominant hues, and their coverage relations. For example, if the statistics show that the references are dominated by high-chroma blue, the compiler requires blue to appear on carrier regions covering a substantial area rather than only as a local accent. • State mapping (structured style evidence + color and luminance distribution → \rightarrow style state S ℛ S_{\mathcal{R}} ). The visual style agent uses the state integration function Ψ \Psi to convert the evidence from the preceding two steps into a unified style state S ℛ = ( M ℛ , A ℛ , T ℛ , L ℛ ) S_{\mathcal{R}}=(M_{\mathcal{R}},A_{\mathcal{R}},T_{\mathcal{R}},L_{\mathcal{R}}) : – Categorization: Rendering fields are written to M ℛ M_{\mathcal{R}} . Color roles, carrier surfaces, and color/luminance statistics are written to A ℛ A_{\mathcal{R}} . Transferable spatial tendencies are written to T ℛ T_{\mathcal{R}} . Subjects, props, scenes, and concrete enclosing structures are written to L ℛ L_{\mathcal{R}} . – Abstraction: Carrier descriptions tied to the reference content are rewritten as transferable visual mechanisms, while the original carriers are retained in L ℛ L_{\mathcal{R}} . For example, “segmented curved illumination on a window” is abstracted as “segmented curved luminous organization”. – Fusion and policy annotation: Color descriptions in the structured style evidence are merged with the color and luminance statistics, and each record is annotated as preserve, weaken, or exclude. For example, if the structured evidence describes a warm color as a local highlight and the color statistics also show that it is concentrated in a small region, the “local highlight” color record is preserved while its concrete carrier is marked as reference content and excluded. • Prompt compilation (style state S ℛ S_{\mathcal{R}} → \rightarrow style prompt p ℛ p_{\mathcal{R}} ). Compilation rewrites the structured fields of the style state into natural-language style instructions usable for image generation. The visual style agent invokes the prompt compiler C C , which follows the fixed ordering π \pi to compile the transferable state into p ℛ p_{\mathcal{R}} : it first describes the overall rendering manner, then the scope in which that manner operates, and finally the colors and their carriers. The composition state T ℛ T_{\mathcal{R}} appears only as a weak hint. Before generation, the agent checks that p ℛ p_{\mathcal{R}} contains none of the subjects, props, scenes, or concrete enclosing structures in L ℛ L_{\mathcal{R}} , and that all extracted rendering practices and color allocations have been written into the style prompt. Once the checks pass, the agent concatenates p ℛ p_{\mathcal{R}} with the generation prompt c c and feeds the result to the generator G G to obtain x x . 4 Experiments 4.1 Experiment Setup We evaluate StyleForge on MegaStyle-1.4M ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , a diverse testbed for style transfer. For efficiency, we randomly sample 31 style categories and generate 16 scenes per category for each method, averaging metrics over these scenes. We instantiate the few-step distilled regime with FLUX.2-Klein (4B and 9B), holding its native 4-step inference path and the target prompts fixed across methods. All methods use a resolution of × 1024 1024\!\times\!1024 and the shared set of 16 content prompts. Additional visual results across generators are provided in Appendix A.3 . We compare StyleForge with five baselines: Vanilla SFT, PSO ( Miao et al., 2025 ) , D-OPSD ( Jiang et al., 2026a ) , Direct Style Extraction (DSE), and Reference-Guided Generation (RCG). For quantitative comparison, we use the VLM-based Score ( Jiang et al., 2026a ) and pairwise Win Rate ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) to assess overall style-transfer quality. The former rates each generated image from 1 to 4 according to its adherence to the target content and fidelity to the reference style, while the latter measures the proportion of direct comparisons won by a method. In Figure 3 , StyleForge transfers the reference style more clearly than the baselines: the mountain scene (row 1, column 2) takes on the neon-lit metallic look of the cyberpunk references, and the market scene (row 3, column 2) takes on the bold red-and-black graphic look of its references, including the ink-splash accents. Figure 4 shows a similar conclusion on the 9B backbone: the forest trail (row 1, column 2) keeps the soft golden haze of its references, and the vintage car (row 6, column 2) keeps the soft ink-wash look of its references. Compared with StyleForge, the qualitative results highlight three issues observed in the baseline outputs. (1) Reference content leakage. DSE may introduce objects from the references that are not requested by the target prompt. For example, in Figure 3 (row 1, column 7), it generates a cyberpunk woman even though the prompt asks only for a mountain range at sunrise with a lake, clearly carrying reference content into the output. (2) Weak style preservation. Baselines often fail to retain distinctive visual cues from the references. For example, in Figure 3 (row 1, columns 3–6), D-OPSD, PSO, Vanilla SFT, and RCG render a generic sunrise landscape instead of the neon-lit metallic look of the cyberpunk references. (3) Degraded few-step generation. Adaptation-based baselines often blur outputs or lose high-frequency detail under few-step generation. For example, in Figure 3 (row 2, columns 3–5), D-OPSD, PSO, and Vanilla SFT reduce the ramen scene to diffuse orange blobs, erasing bowl edges and noodle structure. To connect this knowledge with the visual characteristics of a target style, we introduced StyleForge, which expresses the interplay of rendering, color, and light as coherent guidance for image synthesis. By separating these relationships from the particular subjects and scenes in the references, the framework makes the guidance reusable as the requested content changes. This capacity to carry style across content is reflected in our evaluation, where StyleForge improves transfer quality while maintaining a strong balance between stylistic fidelity and content adherence, with the generator retaining its few-step synthesis capability. Taken together, these results highlight the importance of how style is represented when drawing on pretrained visual knowledge, and support explicit language-based guidance as a practical complement to model adaptation.
